text:
Recent work supports validating diagnostic probes through deliberate faults before using them to guide training. A [2024 recommender metamorphic-testing study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107410) evaluated relations across LibRec, PREA and Surprise, showing that output relationships can expose reliability problems without exact expected predictions. A [2025 mutation-testing study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2025.107807) further assessed relation effectiveness and sensitivity across test inputs. Temporal leakage deserves explicit coverage: a [RecSys 2025 study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3759329) reported sampled nDCG@10 reductions of 21.7–73.4% under a leakage-preventing split. These findings motivate diagnostic checks; they do not establish their validity for NextItNet.

A bounded NextItNet suite is a proposed application of these methods: temporarily replace final-position readout with the incorrect count-minus-one index on left-padded histories; inject future-token dependence into causal intermediate outputs using training-only sequences; disable dilated-convolution residual branches; and apply positive score scaling. Include unchanged-model reruns and restoration checks. Positive scaling should preserve rankings and HR@10, while scale-dependent statistics may change; perturbing future tokens should leave earlier causal features unchanged. Predeclare expected probe responses and thresholds, then report detection sensitivity by fault, false-positive rate and specificity on controls, severity-response curves, and runtime. Exclude interventions that produce no measurable behavioral change from effective-fault counts. Keep weights, splits, seeds and candidate sets fixed, restore interventions immediately, and train no additional predictor. This measures diagnostic validity, without establishing validation gains or proving that a muted branch is unnecessary after retraining.
